abstract.p: Neutralizing antibodies (NAbs) against adeno-associated virus (AAV) represent a significant obstacle to the efficacy of systemic recombinant AAV vector administration or re-administration. While there are some promising preclinical immunomodulation strategies in development, insights into which B cell subsets and compartments maintain persistent AAV NAb may define the optimal eradication strategy. Given the limited success of CD20-directed monotherapy in previous studies, we hypothesized that CD19-directed approaches that extend targeting into the plasma cell compartments may improve AAV NAb eradication. We tested this approach in mice using chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cells or monoclonal antibodies (mAbs). We observed that combination mAbs targeting CD19, CD22, CD20, or B220 in mice did not eliminate tissue-resident B cells and, correspondingly, did not deplete pre-existing high titer AAV8 NAb. In contrast, CD19 CAR-T therapy eliminated peripheral and tissue-resident B cells and plasma cells and resulted in a marked reduction or eradication of high titer AAV8 NAb that permitted successful transgene expression following systemic AAV8 re-administration in mice. This successful therapeutic approach in mice identifies the population and location of B cells necessary to reduce or eradicate AAV NAb sufficiently to permit successful transgene expression with systemic AAV vector administration.

Doshi and colleagues demonstrate successful depletion/eradication of pre-existing AAV NAbs with CD19-targeted CAR-T cells in mice. They also demonstrate depletion of tissue-resident B cells and plasma cells is necessary for removal of AAV NAb. This strategy permitted successful systemic redosing of an AAV8 vector.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Adeno-associated virus (AAV) gene therapy approaches offer the opportunity for potentially curative treatment for multiple inherited diseases and are the most clinically validated means of delivering DNA to target cells in vivo.1,2,3 This, combined with the success of multiple clinical trials using AAV vectors for a variety of disorders, has resulted in the rapid expansion of clinical AAV gene therapy.4,5 Consistent with AAV therapeutic success, there are now licensed vectors for spinal muscular atrophy,6 a form of inherited retinopathy,7 hemophilia B,8,9 hemophilia A,10 a neurometabolic disorder,11 and Duchenne muscular dystrophy.12 Although AAV is now a bona fide novel therapeutic drug class, there remain obstacles to the continued success of AAV-mediated gene therapy, including variability of clinical responses with a wide range of transgene-product levels; the durability of transgene expression concerns in some disease models13,14,15; and immune responses to the viral capsid and/or encoded therapeutic protein that require further attention.16

One of the greatest obstacles to the efficacy of systemic AAV vector administration or re-administration is the presence of neutralizing antibodies (NAbs) against AAV. AAV NAbs represent a subset of the total antibodies (TAbs), which bind AAV. Anti-AAV antibodies are problematic as they limit or preclude the efficacy of systemic AAV vector administration by interfering with cell surface binding and/or causing reticuloendothelial vector clearance preventing target cell transduction.8,17,18,19,20,21,22 A lack of assay standardization prevents direct comparisons between studies, but multiple groups have demonstrated that multi-serotype cross-reactive NAbs develop after environmental exposure to wildtype AAV (wt-AAV) and/or after AAV vector administration.23,24,25,26,27 Specifically, environmental exposure results in approximately 50% prevalence of AAV NAb by 2 years of age and these NAbs persist life-long.23,28,29 Most AAV clinical trials and licensed product labels exclude patients with NAb or TAb against AAV. While titer thresholds vary, acceptable titers for vector infusion (e.g., <1:1, <1:5 NAbs, or <1:50 TAbs) are typically lower than titers observed post environmental AAV exposure.19,30,31 Thus, pre-existing NAbs are the most common reason for ineligibility to receive an AAV vector.

AAV NAbs that develop after AAV vector infusion are typically at least an order of magnitude higher than NAb resulting from environmental exposure to wt-AAV.18,19,30,32,33,34 Additionally, we previously demonstrated that high-titer, multi-serotype cross-reactive NAbs that develop after AAV vector infusion persist for up to 15 years.25 Analogous observations have been made in humans and non-human primates (NHPs) by others.22,32,35,36 Available data suggest that systemic vector infusion in the setting of high titer AAV NAb is unlikely to be efficacious due to failed target tissue transduction.37,38 This is particularly relevant for patients who will be ineligible for repeat vector administration should therapeutic transgene expression be (1) clinically insufficient, (2) not durable after the initial AAV therapy, or (3) if a superior AAV vector is developed for the same indication. Hence, protocols that effectively eradicate existing AAV NAbs and/or prevent AAV NAb formation during vector administration are desirable.

The anti-AAV immune response involves both innate and adaptive arms of the immune system. The innate immune response to AAV is facilitated by toll-like receptor 9 and MyD88 signaling39,40 followed by activation of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells via antigen presentation on major histocompatibility complexes.41,42 These CD4+ T cells then recruit naive B cells to produce immunoglobulin M (IgM) and then class switch to IgG production. There is accumulating evidence that the viral capsid itself or complexed with IgM can activate complement, which may contribute to complement-mediated toxicities.43 Several strategies have been assessed for their ability to eradicate or prevent AAV NAbs, including plasmapheresis with or without immunoadsorption,44,45 regulatory T cell induction,46 degradation of IgG or IgM with cleaving enzymes,47,48,49 and B cell lysis or depletion approaches.50,51,52 These strategies have had variable success particularly in the setting of titers of greater than 1:100, where the degree of AAV NAb depletion is likely insufficient to permit efficacy with systemic vector administration. None have been demonstrated in humans, making the removal of high AAV NAb titers an unresolved obstacle to the ongoing development of AAV-based therapies.

Insights into which lymphoid organs and B cell compartments maintain persistent AAV NAb titers may help to define the optimal immunosuppressive strategy. Preclinical data suggest that targeting CD20+ B cells is insufficient to remove circulating AAV NAbs50,52,53; thus, targeting CD20- B cell or plasma cell populations using CD19-directed approaches such as monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) or CAR-T cells presents the possibility of eradicating or markedly reducing AAV NAbs. CAR-T cells, which target specific antigens by fusing antigen-recognition domains with cellular activation domains, have been clinically successful in multiple B cell malignancies to date.54,55 Specifically, targeting CD19 has been highly successful in achieving remission in children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia.54,55,56,57 There are also emerging data on the efficacy of CD19-targeting CAR-T cells in autoimmune disorders.58 CD19 CAR-T therapy effectively depletes CD19+ B cell subsets from the bone marrow, spleen, lymph nodes, and lymphoid aggregates.59,60 Given limited success with prior immunotherapies in removing AAV NAbs, CD19-targeted CAR-T cells may provide an effective immunomodulation strategy to eliminate high titer AAV NAbs and illuminate the B cell population to target for AAV NAb eradication or reduction.

Here we report that combination B cell mAbs targeting CD19, CD22, and either CD20 or B220 in mice successfully eliminated peripheral but not marrow or splenic B cells and, correspondingly, did not deplete pre-existing high titer AAV NAb. In contrast, CD19 CAR-T cell therapy eliminated peripheral, splenic, and marrow B cell populations and resulted in a marked reduction or eradication of high titer AAV NAb permitting successful transgene expression after systemic AAV re-administration. These data provide insight into the population and location of B cells necessary to target to reduce or eradicate AAV NAbs to permit successful transgene expression with systemic AAV vector administration and outline a successful therapeutic approach in mice.

sec.title: Depletion of CD19+ B cells with CAR-T cells significantly reduces pre-existing AAV8 NAbs
sec.p:
To determine if CD19 depletion via CAR-T cell therapy could effectively deplete pre-existing AAV NAb, wt C57Bl/6J (B6) mice were injected intravenously with AAV8 at 4 × 1012 vg/kg and then treated 2 weeks later with murine CD19-targeted CAR-T (CART-19) cells or control non-transduced (NTD) T cells (Figure 1A). To enable T cell engraftment, these immunocompetent mice received 5 Gy of irradiation on the day before CAR-T injection. In mice that were treated with AAV8 without CAR-T treatment (n = 5/group), AAV8 NAb titers did not decline in irradiated mice compared with non-irradiated controls (Figure 1B) demonstrating that irradiation alone did not impact AAV8 NAb titers. In the T cell-treated mice, CART-19, but not NTD, resulted in complete peripheral B cell aplasia (Figure 1C). Similar mean anti-AAV8 NAb titers of 1:968 ± 1:966 and 1:484 ± 1:296 were noted at the time of CAR-T treatment in the NTD and CART-19 groups, respectively (Figure 1D). Anti-AAV8 NAb titers in the NTD group continued to rise until week 4 and then plateaued with levels of 1:9,670 ± 1:12,611 at week 10 that were significantly higher compared with the CART-19 group titers of 1:6 ± 1:6 (p < 0.001, mixed-effects model with Dunnett’s correction), with only one mouse demonstrating a titer of greater than 1:10 in the CART-19 group at week 10. Concurrent with depletion of AAV8 NAbs, CART-19 resulted in significant reduction of anti-AAV8 IgG at week 10 at 464.8 ± 914.5 ng/mL versus baseline levels of 17,830 ± 4,733 ng/mL (p < 0.001, paired t test) compared with no change in the NTD group from baseline of 17,963 ± 6,110 to 14,066 ± 2,873 ng/mL (Figure 1E). As expected, anti-AAV8 IgM titers decreased in both groups at week 10, consistent with their typical transient nature following antigen exposure (NTD: 19,004 ± 6,954 ng/mL vs. 2,086 ± 1,609 ng/mL [p < 0.001]; CD19: 13,136 ± 2,815 ng/mL vs. 1,480 ± 588 ng/mL [p < 0.001]; paired t test) (Figure 1F). Given that AAV NAb titers in the NTD group continued to rise for the first few weeks after CAR-T therapy, which could reflect ongoing B cell activation, we also tested a longer duration of 4 weeks between AAV8 injection and CAR-T therapy (Figure S1A). These data again demonstrated that CART-19 therapy reliably reduced or eradicated anti-AAV8 NAb (Figure S1B) and IgG (Figure S1C) at week 10 after CAR-T injection. Together, these data support that CD19+ B cell depletion is sufficient for reducing high titer pre-formed AAV8 NAb.Figure 1
Anti-CD19 therapy effectively eradicates pre-existing AAV8 NAb
(A) Schema of AAV8 immunization and CAR-T therapy. C57Bl/6 mice were immunized with AAV8 at 4 ± 1012 vg/kg two weeks before total body irradiation (XRT) followed by CAR-T infusion. CAR constructs included NTD controls (NTD, o; n = 15) or CD19 (, n = 10). Peripheral blood was collected every 2 weeks. (B) Effect of XRT on AAV8 NAb titers. Mice were immunized with AAV8 followed by no XRT (o, n = 5) or XRT (, n = 5) 2 weeks later and AAV8 NAb titers followed for 4 weeks. (C) Peripheral blood CD19+ B cell quantitation and (D) AAV8 NAb titers after NTD (o) or CD19 () CAR-T therapy. Anti-AAV8 total IgG (E) or IgM (F) ELISAs at week 0 (shaded) or week 10 (clear bars) in NTD (o) or CD19-treated () groups. Dashed line represents detection limit of assay. Data presented as mean ± SD. ∗p < 0.05, ∗∗∗p < 0.001. ns, not significant; (B–D) by mixed-effects model, (E) and (F) by paired t test.

sec.title: CART-19 cell therapy reduces pre-existing AAV8 NAb to enable redosing
sec.p:
To test whether the degree of AAV NAb depletion with CART-19 is sufficient to enable efficient vector re-administration, the same B6 mice were intravenously injected with an AAV8 vector carrying a human factor VIII (FVIII) transgene at 4 × 1012 vg/kg and 4 × 1013 vg/kg at 11 weeks after CAR-T treatment (Figure 2A) and serially monitored for AAV8 NAbs (Figure 2B). Notably, despite redosing with AAV8, the CART-19-treated group maintained AAV8 NAb titers at less than 1:5 for 10 weeks after re-challenge (1:1 ± 1:1) compared with the NTD group, in whom AAV8 NAb titers continued to rise to 1:43,885 ± 1:47,432 at 10 weeks from the second AAV treatment. The trend toward decrease in AAV8 NAb titers in the CART-19 group did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.058), but may result from clearance of antigen-antibody complexes after AAV re-administration. The CART-19 mice still had peripheral B cell aplasia at the time of redosing (Figure 1C). As expected, no expression of human FVIII antigen was detected in the NTD group with pre-existing AAV8 NAbs (Figure 2C). Given that irradiation may affect FVIII antigen expression, FVIII antigen after CART-19 treatment was compared between mice with pre-existing AAV8 NAb (AAV+; from the above experiment) and mice who were not pre-immunized with AAV8 (AAV−; Figure 2C). FVIII antigen expression did not significantly differ between AAV-naïve and AAV-immunized mice who were treated with CART-19 to reduce pre-existing NAb titers (Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn’s correction). In the 4 × 1012 vg/kg group, FVIII antigen was 48.4 ± 38.2 ng/mL in AAV-immunized mice, which did not significantly differ from the 28.4 ± 9.6 ng/mL observed in the AAV-naïve mice. In the 4 × 1013 vg/kg group, FVIII antigen was 133.7 ± 135.7 ng/mL in the AAV-immunized mice and, again, did not significantly differ from the 198.9 ± 100.4 ng/mL observed in the AAV-naïve mice. To further assess if there was equivalent vector transduction in AAV-naïve or AAV-immunized mice given CART-19, we measured vector copy number (VCN) by digital droplet PCR. Consistent with a lack of transduction, VCN in the NTD mice was at the lower limit of detection at 0.13 ± 0.21 VCN/diploid cell. In the CART-19 groups, there was a non-significant trend toward a higher VCN in the AAV-naïve mice compared with the AAV-immunized mice (Figure 2D, Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn’s correction). Overall, although VCN and FVIII antigen values did not significantly differ between AAV-immunized and AAV-naïve animals, a trend toward higher FVIII expression and VCN was observed among AAV-naïve animals. Both AAV-naïve and AAV-immunized animals demonstrated a positive correlation between VCN and FVIII expression with some heterogeneity (Figure S2), which may be related, among other possibilities, to FVIII expression heterogeneity due to well established inefficiencies in FVIII synthesis and secretion.61 In the 4 × 1012 vg/kg AAV8 rechallenge group, VCNs were 2.34 ± 0.56 in AAV-naïve and 0.54 ± 0.32 in AAV-exposed mice. In the 4 × 1013 vg/kg AAV8 rechallenge group, AAV-naïve mice had VCN of 18.73 ± 6.23 versus 8.82 ± 1.60 in the AAV-exposed group. In all CART-19-treated mice, the transgenic T cells were detectable in the bone marrow (Figure 2E) and spleen (Figure 2F) until the study terminal time point of 32 weeks after CAR-T cell injection. These results demonstrate that CART-19 treatment reduces pre-existing high-titer AAV8 NAb to allow effective and efficient vector transduction with the same vector serotype, when administered systemically, to permit transgene expression that did not significantly differ from animals without pre-existing AAV8 NAbs.Figure 2
Anti-CD19 CAR-T effectively depletes AAV8 NAb to permit transgene expression following repeat AAV8 vector infusion
(A) Schema of AAV8 re-challenge. Eleven weeks after NTD (o, n = 11) or CD19 (, n = 7) CAR-T therapy, mice were infused with an AAV8 vector encoding human FVIII at 4 × 1012 (squares) or 4 × 1013 (triangles) vg/kg. In parallel, control mice that were not previously immunized with AAV8 were irradiated and infused with CART-19 and 11 weeks later infused with AAV8-hFVIII at the same doses. (B) AAV8 NAb titer after AAV8 vector re-challenge in NTD mice (o) versus CD19-treated () mice. (C) FVIII antigen expression at week 10 after AAV8 challenge. Previously AAV8-immunized mice (AAV+, open symbols) achieve comparable FVIII antigen levels to previously unimmunized mice (AAV−, closed symbols). NTD mice show no hFVIII expression. (D) AAV VCN at week 10 after AAV8 challenge. Previously AAV8-immunized mice (AAV+, open symbols) achieve comparable VCN to previously unimmunized mice (AAV−, closed symbols). NTD mice demonstrate no VCN. CART-19 cells were persistent in the bone marrow (E) and spleen (F) of injected mice at 32 weeks from initial CAR-T injection. Data presented as mean ± SD. ∗∗∗p < 0.001. ns, not significant; (C) and (D) by Kruskal-Wallis test and (E) and (F) by Mann-Whitney test.

sec.title: Antibody-mediated CD19 depletion does not significantly reduce pre-existing AAV8 NAbs
sec.p:
Given that B cell elimination could be achieved via depleting mAbs, we tested the efficacy of such strategies in reducing pre-existing AAV NAb. B6 mice (n = 4–8/group) were infused with AAV8 at a dose of 4 × 1012 vg/kg and 2 weeks later subjected to weekly injections of mAb cocktails targeting murine CD19 and CD22 with either anti-B22062 given weekly or anti-CD20 mAb given every 3 weeks and compared with isotype controls (Figure 3A). Peripheral Igκ+ B cells were significantly reduced in the anti-CD20 group (255 ± 302 cells/μL; p = 0.01, Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn’s correction) and trended lower in the B220 group (963 ± 884) compared with the control group (4,279 ± 2615) (Figure 3B). Despite peripheral B cell depletion, AAV8 NAb titers did not significantly differ between animals treated with mAbs and isotype controls (Figure 3C).Figure 3
B cell-directed mAbs are insufficient to eradicate AAV8 NAb
(A) Schema of mAb therapy. C57Bl6/J mice were immunized with 4 × 1012 vg/kg AAV8 vector 2 weeks before starting treatment with mAb. Mice were treated in three groups (n = 4–8/group): isotype controls (o), anti-murine CD19 and anti-CD22 (weekly) with anti-CD20 (every 21 days) (), or anti-murine CD19/CD22/B220 weekly (). (B) peripheral blood B cells at 6 weeks from start of mAb therapy. (C) Mice were bled every 2 weeks to follow AAV8 NAb titers. Data presented as mean ± SD. ∗p < 0.05. ns, not significant; (B) by Kruskal-Wallis test and (C) by mixed-effects model.

sec.title: B cell compartments are differentially targeted by mAbs versus CART-19
sec.p:
To investigate why mAb B cell depletion fails to eradicate pre-existing AAV8 NAb, we quantified B cells from the bone marrow (Figure 4A) and spleen (Figure 4B) of mAb-treated mice at the end of the study. While there was a decrease in bone marrow B cells in the CD20 mAb-treated cohort (6,434 ± 1,724 CD19+ B cells/106 lymphocytes; p = 0.009, Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn’s correction) compared with the isotypes (54,385 ± 9,495), there was no difference with the B220-treated cohort (23,677 ± 3,631). There was no difference between isotype (398,520 ± 265,140 B cells/106 lymphocytes), CD20-treated (128,264 ± 84,121), and B220-treated (479,973 ± 145,674) cohorts in splenic B cells (Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn’s correction). We confirmed these findings using immunohistochemical staining for CD20+ B cells in the spleen and lymph nodes in CAR-T cell- and mAb-treated mice at the end of each study (Figure 4C). Compared with NTD, CART-19 mice displayed a complete absence of CD20+ B cells in the spleen and lymph node compartments. In contrast, the mAb isotype, CD20, and B220 groups had detectable CD20+ B cells in both the lymph node and spleen. These data corroborate the B cell flow in Figure 4B. Further, the data suggest that mAbs may not effectively reduce AAV Nab-producing B cells and support the hypothesis that depletion of tissue-resident B cells is necessary for AAV NAb elimination. Consistent with this, CART-19-treated animals demonstrated significantly reduced total B cells and plasma cells in their bone marrow and spleens relative to NTD controls (Figure 5). There was near absence of total B cells in the bone marrow (501,080 ± 131,667 cells/106 lymphocytes vs. 1,309 ± 1,221 cells/106 lymphocytes; p < 0.001 by Mann-Whitney test) (Figure 5A) and spleen (273,963 ± 117,783 cells/106 lymphocytes vs. 1,448 ± 2,873 cells/106 lymphocytes; p < 0.001 by Mann-Whitney test) (Figure 5C) after CART-19 treatment. Similarly, there are significantly fewer plasma cells in the bone marrow (794 ± 357 cells/106 lymphocytes vs. 146 ± 129 cells/106 lymphocytes; p < 0.001 by Mann-Whitney test) (Figure 5B) and spleen (1,468 ± 1,216 cells/106 lymphocytes vs. 23 ± 14 cells/106 lymphocytes; p = 0.01 by Mann-Whitney test) (Figure 5D) of CART-19-treated mice relative to NTD controls. Together, these results support that antibody secreting B cells need to be depleted not just from circulation, but also in tissues (e.g., bone marrow and spleen) to reduce and/or eliminate high titer AAV NAbs.Figure 4
B cell-directed mAbs do not completely deplete B cells from lymphoid organs
At week 8 after mAb treatment, CD19+ B cells from the bone marrow (A) and spleen (B) were quantified by flow cytometry. (C) Hematoxylin and eosin stains of lymph nodes (top) and spleens (bottom) tissue sections from mice treated with (from left to right): NTD CAR, CART-19, isotype control mAb, CD19/CD20/CD22 mAb (), and CD19/CD22/B220 mAb (). HRP stain represents CD20+ B cells by IHC. Scale bars, 100 microns. Data presented as mean ± SD. ∗∗p < 0.01. ns, not significant; (A) and (B) by Kruskal-Wallis test.Figure 5
CD19 CAR therapy depletes bone marrow and splenic B cells
Quantification of total B cells (A) and plasma cells (B) from the bone marrow in NTD mice (o) versus CART-19-treated () mice. Quantification of splenic total B cells (C) and plasma cells (D) in NTD mice (o) versus CART-19 () treated mice. All data obtained at week 32 after CAR-T treatment. ∗p < 0.05, ∗∗∗p < 0.001; (A–D) by Mann-Whitney test. Data presented as mean ± SD.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Pre-existing anti-AAV NAbs are the most common reason to be ineligible for AAV gene therapy. Further, after systemic AAV vector infusion, patients universally develop persistent, high-titer, multi-serotype cross-reactive AAV NAb that are likely to preclude the efficacy of repeat intravenous AAV vector infusion.25,32 Our data support that high-titer AAV NAbs prevent therapeutic transgene expression following repeat AAV vector infusion. Here we demonstrate that pre-formed AAV8 NAb titers of greater than 1:1,000 in mice can be successfully reduced by CD19-targeted CAR-T therapy to titers less than 1:5 and permit transgene expression after systemic AAV delivery, comparable with animals with negative AAV8 NAb. Further, CART-19-treated mice had no increase in AAV8 NAb after systemic AAV8 rechallenge, suggesting that this approach could also be used to prevent de novo AAV NAb formation during the period of CART-19-mediated B cell aplasia. Further, the observation that B cell-targeting mAbs resulted in limited B cell depletion in the spleen, marrow, and lymph nodes and persistence of AAV NAbs supports that deep tissue-resident B cell and plasma cell depletion are necessary to reduce or eliminate AAV NAbs. Together, these data provide preclinical proof of concept that CART-19 therapy may effectively reduce high titer pre-existing AAV NAbs to permit efficacious transgene delivery to target tissue by systemic AAV vector infusion. To our knowledge, this is the first study to report on the efficacy of CD19 targeted CAR-T cell therapy for AAV NAbs and vector re-administration.

Data on the inability of mAb-mediated CD19+ and CD20+ B cell depletion to reduce AAV NAbs are supported by prior studies.52,53 Analogous to our observations, Chen et al.53 used higher doses of the same mAb cocktail and demonstrated insufficient reduction in anti-AAV9 NAb to permit transgene expression after systemic AAV vector re-administration. While the study demonstrated B cell depletion in the spleen, B cells in other compartments (e.g., bone marrow) were not quantified. Further, production of anti-AAV IgM, that waned over time, and persistent anti-AAV IgG correlated with AAV NAb titers, which limited transgene expression after systemic AAV9 readministration.53 Rana et al.52 showed that anti-CD20 treatment concurrent with initial AAV8 exposure was insufficient to permit therapeutic transgene expression with repeat systemic AAV8 infusion. However, anti-CD20 initiated before AAV8 exposure with or without concurrent immunosuppression prevented AAV8 NAb development and permitted transgene expression with systemic AAV8 vector re-administration.52 Although this approach demonstrated promise in animals and in a human subject63 to prevent AAV NAbs, the ability of targeted anti-CD20 mAbs to remove pre-existing circulating NAbs was not assessed. Indeed, anti-CD20-targeting therapies would not be expected to clear B cells that have already differentiated into plasma cells64 and thus may work best in preventing AAV NAb. Prior data assessing the utility of rituximab (anti-CD20) to remove pre-existing AAV NAbs in human samples supported efficacy at NAb titers of less than 1:10, but initial titers of greater than 1:100 were not reduced to less than 1:10, the level needed for effective vector transduction, despite multiple rituximab infusions.50 Further, while the proteasome inhibitor bortezomib by itself failed to reduce pre-existing AAV NAbs in mice to permit redosing,65 concurrent bortezomib (to reduce plasma cells) and anti-CD20 therapy reduced AAV8 NAbs to permit efficacious transgene expression with repeat systemic AAV8 vector infusion.66 In the latter study, consistent with our observations of successful AAV NAb reduction, mice demonstrated B cell aplasia in the spleen and marked reduction of marrow B cells.66 Together, these data support that removal of AAV NAbs from circulation to permit either initial or repeat therapeutic vector administration requires significant tissue-resident B cell and plasma cell depletion or aplasia. The greater tissue penetration of CAR-T cells compared with mAbs for B cell depletion and single administration may improve feasibility of B cell aplasia to enable vector dosing in the setting of high titer AAV NAbs.

Two methods to remove AAV NAbs by endopeptidase cleavage of IgG47,48 have been tested and show promise in animal models, IdeS and IdeZ. Both cleave human IgG passively immunized into mice but do not cleave mouse IgG. IdeZ improved luciferase expression in mice passively immunized with human IgG.48 In seropositive NHP with AAV NAb titers of less than 1:40, IdeZ treatment permitted transgene expression. Importantly, the exact NAb titers of the human sera in this study were not reported and the reported NHP AAV NAb titers (<1:40) were 10- to 100-fold lower compared with our study. IdeS was also studied in mice and NHP.47 AAV NAb titers in mice passively immunized with human IgG dropped from less than 1:30 to less than 1:10 after IdeS treatment. In two NHP with AAV NAb titer of less than 1:40, IdeS treatment permitted AAV-mediated factor IX transgene expression, but AAV NAb, as expected, rebounded after treatment. In the same study, IdeS was also able to reduce high titer AAV NAb from more than 1:1,000 to approximately 1:100 and enabled transient FVIII expression in NHP following a vector dose of 2 × 1012 vg/kg. It is unclear if this level of post-treatment AAV NAbs would permit AAV efficacy in humans; ongoing clinical studies are assessing the role of IdeS in AAV gene therapy recipients with pre-existing AAV NAb (NCT06518005 and NCT06241950) and will certainly inform this question. The data on IgG cleaving enzymes largely support their efficacy with comparatively lower endogenous NHP NAb titers (generally <1:100) compared with the mice in our cohorts (1:95–1:3,300). Notably, AAV NAb of greater than 1:1,000 are commensurate with AAV NAb titers observed after AAV infusion by multiple groups19,32,33,34 and with clinical thresholds demonstrated to prevent high-dose systemic AAV efficacy in a clinical trial.8 One limitation of IdeS and IdeZ is that they do not cleave IgM, which can prevent vector transduction; other investigators52 have seen persistent anti-AAV IgM for several weeks after AAV administration. Here, there was low-level persistence of anti-AAV8 IgM at 12 weeks after AAV administration, but the IgM levels did not correlate with neutralization potential or subsequent FVIII antigen production. The mechanism for this persistent IgM is unclear but considerations include ongoing antigen presentation or enhanced survival of innate-like or extrafollicular B cells from elevated B cell-activating factor (BAFF) levels in the setting of B cell depletion resulting in low-affinity IgM. This B cell effect is seen in autoimmune disease67 and a study where concurrent BAFF depletion with immunomodulation was shown to reduce the AAV IgM and splenic plasmablasts.68 CD19 depletion with CAR-T cells is agnostic to IgG or IgM antibody secreting cells, and thus further modifications could clear both from the circulation and prevent the activation of B cells and consequent IgM production if given before infusion. As AAV-IgM complexes could trigger complement responses and subsequent toxicity,69,70 the ability to clear IgM in addition to IgG may provide additional clinical benefit. A recently described modified enzyme (IceMG)49 can cleave both IgM and IgG; in mouse studies, this enzyme enables vector transduction in human IgG immunized mice, but human studies have not been reported.

Our study does have some limitations. First, we only assessed anti-AAV8 antibody responses in mice. Consequently, it is possible that capsids with different tissue tropism may generate different B cell compartment responses and not require such stringent tissue-resident B cell depletion. However, data from other approaches in mice have also analyzed AAV8 and AAV9 vectors and support our conclusions.52,53,65 Second, while mice are an established preclinical immunological model, the relevance of these findings to humans remains to be determined. Third, our study is only designed to assess the efficacy of CART-19 to remove AAV NAbs and enable systemic AAV delivery and did not assess the possibility of differential transduction patterns in the presence or absence of AAV NAb. It is likely that systemic TAb/NAb have a minimal effect on vector transduction in the setting of local delivery especially in immune-privileged sites like the eyes and central nervous system.71,72,73,74,75 Further, our model, which utilizes total body irradiation as preconditioning before T cell infusion, raises an important question regarding the role of the conditioning regimen. Our study demonstrates no diminution of AAV NAbs by irradiation at a dose (5 Gy) that provides effective lymphodepletion and supports robust CAR-T engraftment. While this suggests that clinical conditioning regimens such as cyclophosphamide alone or with fludarabine will also have minimal impact on AAV NAbs, this needs to be evaluated in human studies. While the prolonged humoral immunosuppression with a potent CAR-T product may be a limitation, in recent autoimmune CART-19 trials the duration of B cell depletion is approximately 110 days.76 Approaches that limit CAR-T durability (e.g., the steroids used in AAV gene therapy trial protocols) may shorten the duration of humoral immunosuppression from CAR-T. Finally, although this approach may be promising at eradicating AAV NAbs, potential clinical considerations would need to carefully weigh the risks and benefits, including the possibility of prolonged B cell aplasia,77 the risk of insertional genotoxicity,78 conditioning regimen-associated secondary malignancy risk,79 and the cost of current CAR-T therapies against the severity of the inherited disorder for which gene therapy is being considered. Future approaches that transiently deplete peripheral and tissue-resident CD19+ B cells that do not require conditioning, e.g., mRNA-based CAR-T cell therapy, could improve the risk-benefit profile that would be particularly important for non-fatal disorders like hemophilia.

In summary, our data show that potent B cell depletion with CART-19 therapy can significantly reduce pre-existing AAV NAbs to levels that permit vector re-administration and therapeutic transgene production. These data support the need for the tissue-level depletion of antibody-secreting B cells in the spleen, marrow, and lymph nodes to effectively clear high titer AAV NAbs. The data also support that the failure of previously studied immunosuppressive regimens for a high-titer AAV NAb may be due to persistence of splenic and marrow plasma cells and B cells. In addition, our data support that B cell depletion with CART-19 before AAV treatment prevents new AAV NAb development. Given the success of CD19 CAR-T cells in both malignant and autoimmune diseases,56,76 this strategy or an approach achieving the same effect but transiently, may be translatable to clinical application to overcome the limitations of AAV NAb. In summary, our data support that depletion of both circulating and tissue-resident CD19+ B cells permit reduction/eradication of AAV NAb and TAb to permit either initial treatment or repeat AAV vector administration and provide insight into the mechanisms for persistence of AAV NAb.

sec.title: AAV constructs
sec.p: Human B-domain deleted F8 cDNA was cloned into a previously described pAAV plasmid containing a modified transthyretin promoter, synthetic intron, and AAV2 inverted terminal repeats flanking the expression cassette.80 Recombinant AAV8 vectors were generated and titered via HEK293 triple transfection by the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia Research Vector Core per previously described methods.80 Vectors were stored at −80°C until use.

sec.title: CAR constructs
sec.p: The anti-murine CD19 CAR vector was constructed using the MSGV retrovirus vector system. The second-generation CAR comprised a single-chain variable fragment based on the 1D3 antibody clone, linked to CD28 signaling domain and the CD3ζ signaling domain in which ITAMs 1 and 3 were mutated as previously described.81

sec.title: CAR-T cell production
sec.p: Spleens were harvested from 8- to 12-week-old donor mice and then mashed through a 40-μm filter. The filter was then washed with T cell media (TCM, RPMI 1640 medium [Gibco] with 1% GlutaMAX [Gibco], 10% fetal bovine serum [FBS, Sigma-Aldrich], 1% HEPES [Gibco], 1% NaPyruvate [Thermo Fisher Scientific], 1% nonessential amino acid [Thermo Fisher Scientific], and 1% 55 mM 2-mercaptoethanol [Gibco]). T cells were isolated using a mouse T cell Isolation Kit (STEMCELL Technologies) following the manufacturer’s instructions. The T cells were cultured at 1 million/mL in TCM with recombinant mouse interleukin-2 (IL-2, 100 IU/mL, R&D Systems) and CD28/CD3 beads (Thermo Fisher Scientific) that were added at a 1:1 bead to cell ratio. Two days later, cells were transduced with retroviral vectors by spinoculation. Retrovirus supernatants were seeded into wells pre-coated with retronectin according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Takara Bio) and centrifuged for 1 h at 2,000 rpm. T cells were seeded onto the wells and centrifuged briefly. The next day, cells were counted and passed to a concentration of 0.8 × 106/mL with the addition of IL-2 and some cells were taken for analysis of CAR expression by flow cytometry. The next day, cells were used for in vitro and/or in vivo experiments.

sec.title: Animal models
sec.p: Animal studies were approved by the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee. The wt C57Bl/6J recipient (“B6”) and C57Bl/6 CD45.1 (“PepBoy”) donor mice were obtained from Jackson Laboratory. All studies were conducted with male, littermate controls aged 8–12 weeks at the time of study enrollment.

For CART-19 cell depletion experiments, T cells were isolated from the spleens of PepBoy male mice for lentiviral transfection as described above. B6 CAR-T cell recipient mice were immunized with an AAV8 vector at 4 × 1012 vg/kg 2 weeks before irradiation (5 Gy), which was followed by injection of 4 × 106 CD19 or NTD CAR T cells (Figure 1A). Eleven weeks after CAR-T injection, mice were rechallenged with an AAV8-hFVIII vector at 4 × 1012 and 4 × 1013 vg/kg (Figure 2A). Peripheral blood was collected from the retroorbital plexus every 2 weeks for peripheral flow cytometry, and quantification of anti-AAV NAb and hFVIII antigen.

For antibody depletion experiments, B6 mice were immunized with an AAV8 vector at 4 × 1012 vg/kg two weeks before starting mAb therapy. Animals were treated with anti-CD19 (150 μg/ms weekly) and anti-CD22 (150 μg/ms weekly) with either anti-B220 (150 μg/ms weekly) or anti-CD20 (250 μg/ms every 21 days).62 Anti-CD19, CD22, and B220 (InVivo Mab) antibodies were diluted in PBS and injected intraperitoneally whereas anti-CD20 (Biolegend) diluted in PBS was given via lateral tail vein injection. Isotype control antibodies diluted in PBS were injected in the same manner for the control group. Peripheral blood was collected from the retroorbital plexus every 2 weeks for AAV NAb titers and B cell quantitation.

AAV vectors were diluted to 200 μL final volumes in PBS/Pluronic F-68 and infused via lateral tail vein injection. Peripheral blood for plasma was collected into 3.8% sodium citrate (9:1 vol/vol) and isolated by centrifuging citrated blood for 10 min at 10,000 ×g at 4°C and stored at −80°C until ready to use.

sec.title: Cell isolation
sec.p: Peripheral blood was collected from the retroorbital sinus into EDTA tubes and after staining with flow antibodies, red blood cells lysed with FACSLyse (Invitrogen). At the end of the study, bone marrow and spleens were harvested from each mouse. Spleens and marrows were mechanically fragmented into RPMI-1640 media supplemented with 10% FBS and 100 U/mL penicillin and streptomycin. The resulting cell suspensions were passed through a 70-μm filter followed by red blood cell lysis with ACKLysis buffer (Quality Biological). After centrifugation, cells were resuspended in PBS with 2 mM EDTA and 2% FBS.

sec.title: Flow cytometry
sec.p: Flow cytometry was performed using antibodies listed in Table S1. Cell aggregates (FSC-A vs. FSC-H) were excluded from all analyses. Peripheral blood was stained with appropriate dilutions of antibodies for 20 min at 4°C. Countbright beads (Invitrogen) were added to each tube to normalize collection data. At the end of study, 2 × 106 bone marrow or splenic cells were stained with the corresponding antibody cocktail (Table S1) for 15 or 10 min, respectively, at 4°C. Marrow and splenic cells were washed twice before analysis. All data were acquired on an LSR-Fortessa cytometer (BD Biosciences) and analyzed using FlowJo software (BD Biosciences).

sec.title: Immunohistochemistry
sec.p: Tissue samples were fixed in 10% formalin solution, embedded in paraffin blocks, and cut into 5-μm sections. Immunohistochemistry for CD20 (Abcam), staining was carried out using the Vector ImmPRESS Polymer System, Peroxidase (HRP) Substrate. After de-paraffinization, antigen retrieval was carried out by boiling the slides in tris-based, pH 9 (Vector) for 20 min. Antibodies at optimal dilution were incubated overnight at 4°C. Slides were then incubated with anti-rabbit HRP polymer for 30 min at room temperature followed by DAB+ substrate-chromogen solution for 5 min at room temperature. Slides were counterstained with hematoxylin and mounted.

sec.title: AAV8-NAb assay
sec.p: An in vitro transduction inhibition assay was used to quantify the titer of AAV8 NAb from mouse plasma using an AAV8 Renilla Luciferase reporter vector. We coated 2V6.11 cells, which stably express the adenovirus E4 gene to enable transduction by AAV vectors, onto 96-well plates at 20,000 cells/well in complete DMEM (10% FBS, 1% antibiotic/antimycotic, 1% L-glutamine) supplemented with 1 μg/mL of ponasterone A. Plasma samples were serially diluted and incubated with the reporter vector and this mixture used to transduce 2V6.11 cells at a multiplicity of infection of approximately 281 vg/cell. After 24 h, luciferase expression is measured using the Renilla Luciferase Assay System and a GloMax Navigator plate reader (Promega).82 To calculate a precise AAV NAb titer, serial dilutions versus percent luciferase expression (compared with no serum control) were fit with linear regression and 50% inhibition extrapolated from these curves.

sec.title: AAV IgG and IgM ELISA
sec.p: Anti-AAV8 IgG and IgM were quantified by ELISA. AAV8 capsids were coated at 1 × 1011vg/mL in 0.2 M sodium bicarbonate (pH 9.5) overnight at 4°C. Standard wells were coated with mouse IgG (Sigma I-5381) or IgM (Sigma M-3795) directly in coating buffer overnight. Unbound capsids or standards were washed with PBS +0.05% Tween 20. Wells were blocked with 3% BSA in PBS/Tween for 4 h at 4°C before addition of plasma samples, which were incubated overnight at 4°C. After another wash, detection antibodies for IgG (goat anti-mouse IgG HRP, Southern Biotech 1030-05) at 1:5,000 dilution or IgM (goat anti-mouse IgM HRP, Southern Biotech 1140-05) at 1:8,000 dilution were added for 2 h at 37°C and detected with OPD substrate solution. Absorbance at 490 nm was measured on a SpectraMax M5 plate reader (Molecular Diagnostics). The 95% confidence interval for the negative control (i.e., detection limit) for IgG was 117–429 ng/mL and for IgM was 272–505 ng/mL.

sec.title: Human FVIII antigen ELISA
sec.p: Plasma FVIII antigen circulating in AAV-treated mice was determined by ELISA using matched-pair antibodies against human FVIII (Affinity Biologicals).83 Two modifications were made to the manufacturer’s protocol: wells were coated with primary capture antibody overnight at 4°C and well volumes were reduced by one-half (e.g., 50-μL sample volume). Standard curves were prepared with recombinant protein (purification as described in Wilhelm et al.84) reconstituted in plasma collected and pooled from untreated mice of the appropriate strain. Standards and mouse plasma samples were diluted 10-fold in green dilution buffer before plating in duplicate. Sample FVIII antigen was determined by converting absorbance at 490 nm using the sample’s respective standard curve. Measured values below background were assigned a value of 0.

sec.title: AAV VCN determination
sec.p: Livers were homogenized using a Qiagen TissueLyser LT bead-mill and gDNA was extracted using a Qiagen AllPrep DNA/RNA Kit. DNA was quantified using NanoDrop Microvolume Spectrophotometer, and 150 ng was double digested with NotI and SacII using NEB cutsmart 2.1 buffer for 1 h at 37°C followed by a 5 min heat inactivation at 65°C. Digital droplet PCR was conducted using 0.75× of FAM-conjugated primer to specifically detect human F8 with an Ap3b1 HEX referenced primer referenced primer as previously described80 and 18.5 ng double-digested DNA. Droplets were read individually analyzed on a QX200 Droplet Reader using QX Manager Software (BioRad). VCN was calculated in BioRad QuantaSoft Software.

sec.title: Statistical analyses
sec.p: All data were analyzed using GraphPad Prism version 10. D’Agostino-Pearson normality tests were used to determine distribution of data before analysis and non-parametric analyses were used when data were not normally distributed. Longitudinal data were analyzed by mixed-effects ANOVA with correction for multiple comparisons to account for variation by animal and time point. Endpoint data were analyzed with the Mann-Whitney U test for two groups or Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn’s correction for multiple comparisons. Anti-AAV8 IgG and IgM levels were compared by paired two-tailed t tests. An alpha of 0.05 was used as the cutoff for statistical significance. All data are presented as mean ± SD and graphed with errors bars representing the SD.

sec.title: Data availability
sec.p: All original data are available from the authors upon request.
